passage: In the small house near the paddy fields outside Kottayam, Joseph had spent the first year of his distance-learning degree studying at midnight and waking at eleven, groggy, missing the morning bus to the study centre. In June he decided to change it himself. Lights off by half past ten, up with the church bell at six, two hours of study before the heat. He drew a table in the back of an old notebook and marked each day: sleep time, wake time, pages done. His sister Reena teased him about the chart. By August the columns were full of neat ticks, and his unit test score had jumped. He showed Reena the notebook, flipping page after page. "I did all this," he said, almost surprised.

qa.q: What did Joseph mark in the table each day?
qa.a: Sleep time, wake time and pages done.

qa.q: Why was Joseph almost surprised when he said "I did all this"?
qa.a: After a year of drifting, he hadn't quite believed his own choices could change things; the full pages of ticks proved they had.

qa.q: Which choice helped Joseph stick to the new schedule?
qa.a: Tying wake-up to the church bell and recording every day, so progress was visible and each tick encouraged the next.

qa.q: How might Reena's view of the chart change by August?
qa.a: Reena, who teased him at first, may be impressed to see page after page of ticks and a better test score.

grounding: A student sets his own sleep and study routine, records it, and sees results that show he shaped the outcome.

passage: Tomas started his second year in Valencia with a rule he made for himself: bed by midnight, library from nine to twelve, no exceptions for five weeks. His roommate Mateo bet him a paella that he wouldn't last a fortnight. Tomas made a spreadsheet and filled in every day: hours slept, hours studied, and one line on how he felt. The first week was rough. By week three the numbers settled, and his notes started making sense. In week five his statistics quiz came back with the best mark he'd ever had. He scrolled through the spreadsheet slowly, row after row of small green cells. "I built this," he told Mateo. Mateo paid for the paella.

qa.q: What did Mateo bet Tomas?
qa.a: A paella, that he wouldn't last a fortnight.

qa.q: How did Tomas feel scrolling through the spreadsheet after the quiz?
qa.a: Proud and a bit amazed; the rows of green cells showed him that his steady choices had built the best mark he'd ever had.

qa.q: What choice kept Tomas going through the rough first week?
qa.a: Recording every day, including how he felt, so he could watch the numbers settle instead of judging the plan too early.

qa.q: How might Mateo feel paying for the paella?
qa.a: Mateo lost the bet but may be happy to, having watched a roommate prove Mateo wrong through five weeks of effort.

grounding: A student fixes his sleep and study routine, tracks it daily, and his results show he is the author of the change.

subtype: Everything is luck or teacher's mood [Actor]
passage:
Class 5 teacher's note, Deepika, 12 August
Trisha got 9 out of 25 in the science test again. When I gave the paper back, she said, "You always give me low marks, ma'am. Riddhi is lucky, you like her." I asked how she had studied. She said she hadn't, because "it doesn't matter, it depends on your mood". She says this after almost every test. On the one test she did revise for, the plants chapter in July, she got 21, but when I reminded her, she said the questions were "just easy that day". I am worried she has stopped trying.
What I did next: I asked her to revise one short topic with me on Wednesday, and we will put the two marks side by side to see what changed.

qa.q: What did Trisha get on the plants chapter test she revised for?
Why does Trisha say the marks depend on the teacher's mood?
qa.a: Believing results come from outside feels easier than linking them to her own preparation; it also spares her the worry that revising might not help.

qa.q: What choice by Deepika could help Trisha see the link to effort?
qa.a: Revising one short topic together and putting the marks side by side, so Trisha sees for herself what preparation changes.

qa.q: How might Riddhi feel if she heard she was only "lucky"?
qa.a: Riddhi might feel her own hard work had been dismissed, and a little hurt at being called the teacher's favourite.

grounding: A child explains low marks as the teacher's mood or luck and never connects them to preparation.

subtype: Everything is luck or teacher's mood [Actor]
passage: In the one-room school at Khandala, the spelling results were read out every Saturday. Ganga, who was nine, got four out of ten again. "The teacher reads too fast when it's my turn," she told her neighbour Farhan on the walk home, kicking a stone. "And she gives the hard words to me. It's bad luck." Farhan, eleven, said nothing for a while. He had seen her spelling list lying under the bangle box all week, never opened. "Last month you practised with your Ammi and got nine," he said. Ganga shrugged. "That was easy-words day." She walked faster, ahead of him, swinging her bag.

qa.q: What did Ganga score in the spelling test?
qa.a: Four out of ten.

qa.q: Why does Ganga call it bad luck rather than practice?
qa.a: Blaming the teacher's speed and the hard words protects her from feeling she could have done better, and makes practising seem useless.

qa.q: What could help Ganga link her marks to practice?
qa.a: Practising the list with her Ammi again before the next Saturday and comparing the scores, so she can see the difference herself.

qa.q: How might Farhan feel when Ganga walks ahead of him?
qa.a: Farhan may feel awkward or brushed off, since he was only pointing out something true and she doesn't want to hear it.

grounding: A child in a village school blames spelling marks on the teacher and luck, ignoring the unopened list.

passage:
"Anjali, why are you awake? It's past midnight."
"Papa, is it because of my fees?"
Joseph sat on the edge of her bed. "Is what because of your fees?"
"You and Mama. Shouting. It started after the tuition fees went up. If I'd got the scholarship, you wouldn't fight."
"Mole, no."
"And last week, when Mama cried, that was after I broke the mixer."
"Anjali, listen. Mama and I are arguing about many things. Work, your grandmother's house, money. Grown-up things. Not you."
"But if I just did everything right..."
"Then we would still argue. You can't carry this. It isn't yours to fix."
She pulled the sheet up to her chin. "It feels like mine."
"I know. I'm sorry it does. Tomorrow Mama and I will both tell you this. Together."

qa.q: What did Anjali break before Mama cried?
qa.a: The mixer.

qa.q: Why does Anjali believe the fights are her fault?
qa.a: They began after the fees went up, so she links them to herself; believing she caused it also means she could fix it by doing everything right, which feels less helpless.

qa.q: What choice by Joseph helps Anjali most?
qa.a: Naming the real reasons as grown-up matters and planning to tell her together with Mama, so the message is clear and shared.

qa.q: How does Joseph feel when Anjali says "It feels like mine"?
qa.a: He is sorry and sad that his daughter has been carrying this, and wants to lift it off her rather than argue with her feelings.

grounding: A teenager blames herself for her parents' arguments, and her father explains that it is not hers to carry.

passage: When Samir got caught copying in the physics exam last month, I didn't sleep for two nights. The thing is, a week earlier he'd asked me to study with him and I'd said no, because I had cricket selection. So in my head it was simple: if I'd said yes, he'd have learned it, he wouldn't have copied, he wouldn't be suspended. My fault. I kept replaying it. I even went to the principal to say I should have helped him. The principal just looked at me kindly and said, "Kunal, Samir made a choice. You can care about him without owning it." I'm still thinking about that. I can be a good friend. I can't be the one who decides for him.

qa.q: Why did Kunal say no when Samir asked to study together?
qa.a: Because of cricket selection.

qa.q: Why did Kunal feel responsible for the suspension?
qa.a: Kunal linked one refusal to Samir's copying and imagined having the power to prevent it, which turned care for a friend into heavy guilt.

qa.q: What turning point helped Kunal see it differently?
qa.a: The principal's words, "Samir made a choice. You can care about him without owning it", which separated friendship from responsibility.

qa.q: How might Samir feel if he knew Kunal felt to blame?
qa.a: Samir might feel uncomfortable or sorry, since the copying was his own decision, and may not want his friend carrying it.

grounding: A teenager takes the blame for a friend's decision to copy, until seeing that the choice was the friend's.

passage:
Counsellor's note, Sunaina, Grade 9, 20 November
Vikas asked to see me after assembly. His class teacher had mentioned he'd gone quiet and his marks were slipping, and today he told me why: his parents have been arguing a lot, and he believes it is because of him. "If I didn't need so much, if I got better marks, they'd be okay." He listed his "mistakes" in detail. He looked exhausted. I asked if he feels safe at home; he said yes, it's the shouting and the silence afterwards. I told him clearly that adults' arguments are the adults' responsibility, not his. What I did next: with his agreement, I called his mother this afternoon, and the three of us will meet on Friday. I'll check in with Vikas every day this week.

qa.q: When will Sunaina, Vikas and his mother meet?
qa.a: On Friday.

qa.q: Why might Vikas believe his parents' arguments are his fault?
qa.a: If the fights are his doing, he could stop them by needing less and scoring more; that feels less helpless than accepting he can't control them, but it leaves him exhausted with guilt.

qa.q: What choice by Sunaina helps lift the weight from Vikas?
qa.a: Saying plainly that the arguments are the adults' responsibility, checking he is safe, and bringing his mother into a meeting so the message comes from home too.

qa.q: How might Vikas's mother react to the counsellor's call?
qa.a: She may be shocked and sad to learn her son blames himself, and glad of the chance to tell him directly that it isn't his fault.

grounding: A counsellor notes a teenager who blames himself for his parents' fights and responds the same day.

subtype: Balanced view of luck and effort [Response]
passage: The B.Sc. results were pasted outside the college office in Sagar. Tanuja found her name: a pass in chemistry, but lower than she'd hoped. Zeenat, beside her, was fuming. "That paper was unfair. Everyone says it was the toughest in years." Tanuja nodded slowly. "It was tough. That wasn't in my hands." She thought about the organic unit she'd skimmed because it bored her, and the three questions from it she'd left blank. "But I also skipped organic. That part was mine." On the bus home, past the mustard fields, she wrote in her notebook: "Next sem: organic first, practice papers from the last five years. Tough papers will happen." She felt steadier than she had that morning.

qa.q: What did Tanuja write in her notebook on the bus?
qa.a: "Next sem: organic first, practice papers from the last five years. Tough papers will happen."

qa.q: Why did Tanuja feel steadier by the end of the day?
qa.a: Seeing both the tough paper and the skipped unit let her avoid both blaming others and blaming only herself, and gave her a plan she could act on.

qa.q: Which choice showed a balanced response to the result?
qa.a: Accepting the paper's difficulty as outside her control while owning the skipped organic unit, then planning practice papers.

qa.q: How might Zeenat see the same result differently?
qa.a: Zeenat sees only the unfair paper, which may protect her from disappointment but gives her nothing to change for next time.

grounding: A student sees that both a hard paper and her own skipped unit shaped her result, and acts on the part she controls.

subtype: Balanced view of luck and effort [Response]
passage: At the welcome dinner in Edinburgh, Felix asked Mei how she'd won the scholarship. She started to say "hard work", then stopped. It was true: two years of late nights over maths. But she also thought of her school in Singapore, the well-stocked lab, the teacher who stayed after class, her parents who could afford books. "Honestly? A lot of work and a lot of luck." Felix laughed. "At least you admit the luck." Mei smiled, but that night she made a list. She couldn't choose where she'd grown up. She could choose to go to office hours every week, to volunteer with the tutoring scheme for first-generation students, and to keep up the late nights when they mattered.

qa.q: What was Mei's honest answer to Felix?
qa.a: "A lot of work and a lot of luck."

qa.q: Why did Mei stop before saying only "hard work"?
qa.a: Mei felt uneasy taking all the credit, because she recognised the school, teacher and books she was lucky to have, alongside her own effort.

qa.q: What choices did Mei list, and why do they fit a balanced view?
qa.a: Weekly office hours, volunteering with the tutoring scheme and keeping up the late nights; they act on what she controls without pretending luck played no part.

qa.q: Why might Felix appreciate Mei admitting the luck?
qa.a: Felix may not have had the same advantages, so hearing Mei name them feels honest and respectful of different starting points.

grounding: A student acknowledges both effort and privilege in her scholarship and chooses actions she can control.

subtype: Balanced view of luck and effort [Response]
passage: In the placement cell's waiting room, Yogesh sat with his rejection email open. Dhruv, who'd been placed a week earlier, sat beside him. "The interviewer asked that graph question nobody could solve," Yogesh said. "Three of us got it. All three failed." "Bad luck," Dhruv agreed. Yogesh was quiet. "Yeah. But the first two questions were basic arrays, and I fumbled those too. I haven't practised since June." He opened his notes and typed two lists. "Not mine: which interviewer, which question." "Mine: one hour of practice daily, two mock interviews with the cell before the next company." He showed Dhruv. "This feels less like I'm cursed and less like I'm useless." Dhruv nodded. "Mock tomorrow at four?"

qa.q: What did Yogesh put on the "Mine" list?
qa.a: One hour of practice daily and two mock interviews with the cell before the next company.

qa.q: What does Yogesh mean by feeling "less like I'm cursed and less like I'm useless"?
qa.a: Splitting the result into luck and his own share frees him from blaming fate or himself entirely, which feels lighter and more hopeful.

qa.q: Which choice by Yogesh shows a balanced response to the rejection?
qa.a: Admitting the unlucky graph question while owning the fumbled array questions, then planning practice and mock interviews.

qa.q: How might Dhruv feel being shown the two lists?
qa.a: Dhruv may feel relieved his friend isn't sinking, and glad to help by offering a mock interview the next day.

grounding: A student separates the bad luck of a hard interview question from his own lack of practice, and acts on his share.

passage: Shalini had come home to the village near Madurai after her job interview, sure it was out of her hands now. "If it's in my fate, I'll get it," she said, and stretched out on the thinnai. Her Kavitha chithi was already out in the field, checking the channels before the rain. Shalini watched her all afternoon: pulling weeds, mending a broken bund, talking to the neighbour about seed. At dusk, Chithi lit the lamp before the small shrine and said, as she always did, "Whatever God has written will come." Shalini asked, half teasing, "Then why work so hard?" Chithi laughed. "God writes. I still have to carry the water." That night Shalini opened her laptop and sent the thank-you email she'd been skipping.

qa.q: What did Chithi say when Shalini asked why she worked so hard?
qa.a: "God writes. I still have to carry the water."

qa.q: Why did Shalini feel she could just rest after the interview?
qa.a: Believing the result was already in fate's hands made further effort feel unnecessary, and resting felt like trust rather than avoidance.

qa.q: What choice did Shalini make after watching Chithi?
qa.a: She sent the thank-you email she'd been skipping, doing her own part while still trusting the outcome.

qa.q: How does Kavitha chithi hold faith and effort together?
qa.a: For Chithi, trusting what God has written sits easily beside mending bunds and pulling weeds; the prayer and the work belong to the same day.

grounding: A young adult watches her aunt trust fate and still work hard, and sees that belief need not cancel effort.

passage: Jamal used to think his flatmate Bilal was a contradiction. Before his accountancy exams in Birmingham, Bilal would say, "It's in God's hands, inshallah," and then study at the kitchen table until two in the morning. When the results came, Bilal passed and said, "Alhamdulillah, it was written." Jamal finally asked him about it over tea. "If it's written, why kill yourself studying?" Bilal shrugged. "Trusting God doesn't mean sitting on my hands. I do my part, then I leave the rest." Jamal thought about his own habit of saying "whatever happens, happens" and then not revising. He'd always called it being relaxed. Watching Bilal, it looked more like hiding. The next morning he printed out a study plan of his own.

qa.q: Until what time did Bilal study at the kitchen table?
qa.a: Until two in the morning.

qa.q: Why did Jamal see Bilal as a contradiction at first?
qa.a: Jamal assumed that trusting God with the outcome should make hard study unnecessary, so doing both seemed inconsistent.

qa.q: What turning point led Jamal to print a study plan?
qa.a: Hearing Bilal say he does his part and then leaves the rest, which made Jamal see his own "whatever happens" as hiding rather than calm.

qa.q: How does Bilal see the link between faith and effort?
qa.a: For Bilal they fit together: trust in God covers the outcome, while study is his own responsibility, so he feels no conflict.

grounding: A young man observes his flatmate trusting God and still studying hard, and realises belief need not cancel responsibility.

passage: At the insurance office, Preeti had noticed something about Vijay sir, the senior claims officer. Every morning he touched the small Ganesh idol on his desk and murmured a prayer. When anyone worried about appraisals, he'd say, "Karma will decide." Yet he was the one who stayed back to double-check every file, who taught the juniors the new claims system, who never missed a deadline. One afternoon Preeti asked him, carefully, whether believing in karma didn't make effort pointless. Vijay sir smiled. "Karma is what you do, Preeti. Not what you wait for." She sat with that for a while. She had been telling herself the promotion list was destiny and hadn't updated her training record in months. That evening she stayed back and finished it.

qa.q: What does Vijay sir touch every morning?
qa.a: The small Ganesh idol on his desk.

qa.q: Why had Preeti let her training record slide?
qa.a: Calling the promotion list destiny made her effort feel beside the point, which quietly excused her from updating the record.

qa.q: What choice did Preeti make after the conversation, and why?
qa.a: She stayed back and finished the training record, because Vijay sir's words showed her that faith in karma still asks for action.

qa.q: How does Vijay sir see karma differently from Preeti?
qa.a: For Vijay sir karma is made by what you do, so prayer and hard work go together, while Preeti had treated it as something to wait for.

grounding: A young employee observes a senior colleague who trusts karma yet works diligently, and sees belief need not cancel responsibility.

passage: Bidisha's tea stall near the Bankura bus stand had lost half its customers since spring. "It's the new bakery opposite," she told Lakshmi, who sold flowers beside her. "And the heat. And this year's bad luck, what to do." Lakshmi nodded, but she had seen other things. Bidisha opened at nine now, not seven, and the morning bus crowd had found somewhere else. She had snapped at a regular for asking for less sugar. The cups were chipped. "Maybe open early again?" Lakshmi tried. Bidisha waved it away. "The problem isn't me, didi. Everything is against me this year." She said it almost proudly, like someone refusing to be blamed. By evening she had sold eleven cups.

qa.q: What time does Bidisha open the stall now?
qa.a: At nine, not seven.

qa.q: Why does blaming the bakery, the heat and luck feel reasonable to Bidisha?
qa.a: It protects her pride; admitting that her late opening and sharp words drove customers away would hurt more than blaming things outside her.

qa.q: What turning point did Bidisha brush aside, and what could she try?
qa.a: Lakshmi's suggestion to open early again; reopening at seven for the bus crowd would test whether her own choices matter.

qa.q: How does Lakshmi see Bidisha's falling sales?
qa.a: Lakshmi notices the late opening, the snapping and the chipped cups, and gently hints at them, but is waved away.

grounding: An adult tea-stall owner blames the market and luck for falling sales and never looks at her own role.

passage: Lars had lost his third design client in a year, and over coffee in Oslo he explained it to Daniel. "The first one had an impossible boss. With the second, the market crashed. This one, just bad luck; they changed direction." Daniel listened. He remembered that all three had complained about missed deadlines. "Did any of them say anything about timing?" Lars snorted. "They always say that. It's an excuse." He went on about how the industry was rigged for people with connections. Daniel tried once more. "What would you do differently next time?" Lars looked genuinely confused. "Nothing. It wasn't me." He was smiling, but his jaw was tight.

qa.q: How many design clients had Lars lost in a year?
qa.a: Three.

qa.q: What might Lars's tight jaw suggest behind the smile?
qa.a: He may feel more hurt and defensive than he shows; blaming bosses and luck keeps his pride safe, but the question still stings.

qa.q: What went wrong in the conversation, and what could help Lars learn from the losses?
qa.a: Lars dismissed the deadline complaints as excuses; looking honestly at timing on his next project would let him test his own share.

qa.q: How might Daniel feel after asking twice?
qa.a: Daniel is likely frustrated and concerned, wanting to help a friend who won't look at the one pattern all three clients mentioned.

grounding: An adult blames bosses, the market and luck for losing clients and refuses to examine his own share.

passage: In the small meeting room at the phone showroom, Farhan's quarterly review was not going well. "Sales are down again," said Ganga, the branch manager, sliding the sheet across. "Third quarter in a row." Farhan leaned back. "Ma'am, the market is dead. Online prices are lower. And honestly, the walk-in customers you give me are the worst ones." Ganga pointed to one line. "Your follow-up calls: four this quarter. Ravi made sixty." "Ravi gets lucky customers." "Will you try making more calls next month?" "It won't matter. It's never been about me." He said it firmly, as if closing the subject. Ganga wrote something down and didn't reply.

qa.q: How many follow-up calls did Farhan make this quarter?
qa.a: Four.

qa.q: Why does Farhan insist "It's never been about me"?
qa.a: Admitting the four calls might be part of the problem would hurt his pride, so blaming the market, customers and luck feels safer.

qa.q: What choice could Farhan make to test his belief?
qa.a: Trying more follow-up calls next month, as Ganga suggested, and comparing results, instead of deciding in advance it won't matter.

qa.q: How might Ganga feel when Farhan closes the subject?
qa.a: Ganga is likely frustrated or worried, having offered a clear, fixable point and seen it pushed away.

grounding: A salesperson blames the market, customers and luck for three bad quarters and refuses to examine his own effort.

passage: At the Saturday maths club, Sunaina ma'am held up Vikas's worksheet. "Look, all correct again! Vikas is our little genius." The others clapped. Then she put two stacks on the table: easy puzzles and a new "challenge" set. "Pick whichever you like." Vikas picked the easy ones. He finished in ten minutes and sat drawing. When Meena from his class tried to hand him a challenge puzzle, he pushed it back so hard the paper tore. "I don't want it!" Sunaina ma'am was surprised. At the end she asked him quietly why. Vikas looked at his shoes. "If I get it wrong, then I'm not a genius anymore."

qa.q: What did Sunaina ma'am call Vikas when she held up his worksheet?
qa.a: "Our little genius."

qa.q: Why did Vikas push the challenge puzzle away so angrily?
qa.a: He was scared that getting it wrong would take away the "genius" label; the anger covered his fear of losing it.

qa.q: What could Sunaina ma'am try next time instead of calling him a genius?
qa.a: Praise the way he worked through a problem, and celebrate trying a hard puzzle even if it's wrong, so risk feels safe.

qa.q: How might Meena have felt when the puzzle was pushed back?
qa.a: Meena was trying to share and may have felt hurt or confused by the sudden anger, not knowing it came from fear.

grounding: A child praised as a genius avoids challenging puzzles to protect the label.

passage: I'm Deepak, Mahima's older brother. Since she started reading at four, every relative has called her "our brilliant girl". Nani says it, our uncles say it, Papa says it at every dinner. Lately I've noticed something. When I set up the chess board, Mahima says she's busy. She used to love chess, but last month I beat her twice. She rereads easy storybooks she has already finished instead of the thick one her teacher gave her. Yesterday I asked her to try a crossword with me and she snapped, "I don't like stupid games!" and stomped off. I don't know for sure what's going on in her head. But she only seems to do things she already knows she'll win.

qa.q: What does every relative call Mahima?
qa.a: "Our brilliant girl."

qa.q: What might Mahima be afraid of when she refuses chess and the crossword?
qa.a: She may fear that losing or struggling would prove she isn't brilliant after all, so avoiding hard things protects the label everyone gives her.

qa.q: How could the family's praise change to help Mahima take risks?
qa.a: Praising her effort and the ways she tries, like working out a crossword clue, rather than calling her brilliant, so struggling doesn't feel like failing.

qa.q: How does Deepak feel about the change in his sister?
qa.a: Deepak seems puzzled and a little worried, missing the sister who loved chess, and unsure what is going on inside her.

grounding: An older brother notices his sister, always called brilliant, avoiding any challenge she might not win.

passage:
Monday, first week of term: Chinmay solved the class puzzle first. "You're so smart, Chinmay," the teacher said. Eshaan, next to him, whispered, "Show-off." Chinmay glowed all day.
Thursday, three weeks later: The teacher offered a "tough question" to anyone who wanted extra points. Eshaan tried and got it half right. Chinmay kept his hand down. At home he told his mother the question was boring.
Saturday, a month later: The science quiz had a new kind of problem. Chinmay stared at it, face hot, and left it blank rather than guess. When Eshaan asked how he'd done, he snapped, "Leave me alone!" and walked off. That night he whispered to his mother, "What if I'm not actually smart?"

qa.q: What did the teacher say when Chinmay solved the puzzle first?
qa.a: "You're so smart, Chinmay."

qa.q: What was Chinmay worried about when he whispered to his mother?
qa.a: That struggling with the new problem meant he wasn't really smart; the label had become something he could lose, so every hard question felt like a threat.

qa.q: What went wrong over the month, and what could help Chinmay now?
qa.a: Praise for being smart made him avoid risk; praise for trying new methods, and a calm talk about mistakes being part of learning, could help.

qa.q: How might Eshaan see Chinmay's change over the month?
qa.a: Eshaan saw a show-off at first, then a classmate who won't try and snaps at him, and may feel confused or hurt.

grounding: Over a month, a child praised as smart begins avoiding hard questions to protect the label.

passage:
Tuesday: Ojas got stuck on the fraction word problem and threw his pencil down. Harish sir came over. "What have you tried?" "Nothing works." "Try drawing it," Harish sir said, and moved on.
Wednesday: Ojas tried drawing pizzas. Wrong. Then counting in steps. Wrong. Then a number line, and it worked. Harish sir crouched by his desk. "You tried three different ways, and when the first two didn't work, you switched. That's exactly how people get good at maths."
Friday: When Harish sir offered a harder bonus sheet, Ojas's hand shot up first. "Can I try the number line on these?" He got four out of six, and he was grinning.

qa.q: What method finally worked for Ojas on Wednesday?
qa.a: A number line.

qa.q: Why was Ojas's hand the first to shoot up on Friday?
qa.a: Harish sir's praise showed him that switching methods is how people get good, so he felt confident and eager, seeing a harder sheet as a chance rather than a risk.

qa.q: What made Harish sir's praise work well?
qa.a: It named exactly what Ojas did, trying three ways and switching, rather than calling him clever, so he knew what to repeat.

qa.q: What would change if Harish sir had only said "Good boy, you're clever"?
qa.a: Ojas might not know what helped, and could even avoid the bonus sheet in case it made him look less clever.

grounding: A teacher praises a child's strategy switching, and the child begins seeking harder problems.

passage: Imran, you asked how to encourage the weaker ones in your class. Let me tell you about a girl called Pinki, from my first year teaching in Nagpur, when the children called me Usha teacher. She was nine and she hated long division. One day I watched her try it the book way and fail, then try splitting the number into hundreds and tens and fail, then try guessing and checking, and get it right. Before, I'd have said "good girl, clever girl". That day I said, "Pinki, you tried three ways and didn't give up. That's how you got it." She looked at me as if no one had ever said that to her. The next week she asked for the hard sums. Praise what they did, beta, not what they are.

qa.q: What three ways did Pinki try for long division?
qa.a: The book way, splitting the number into hundreds and tens, and guessing and checking.

qa.q: Why did Pinki look at Usha teacher as if no one had ever said that?
qa.a: She was surprised and moved to be praised for her persistence rather than her cleverness; it showed her that her effort mattered.

qa.q: What choice does Usha urge Imran to make in class?
qa.a: To praise what the children do, their methods and persistence, rather than what they are, so they reach for harder work.

qa.q: How might Imran use this story with the weaker students?
qa.a: Imran might watch for a child trying different approaches and name it aloud, helping that child see progress as something they can build.

grounding: An elder teacher recalls praising a child's methods and persistence, after which the child sought harder problems.

passage: The Class 6 room at the government school had fifty-two students and one fan, and Francis sir had only ten minutes before the bell. Samir was still bent over the geometry problem most had skipped, having tried measuring with a broken ruler, then folding the paper, then drawing a grid on the back. Francis sir, squeezing between benches with forty notebooks still to check, stopped anyway. "Samir, show me." Samir showed the grid. "You tried folding, and when that didn't work you made a grid. That was smart work, not luck." The bell rang. Samir packed slowly, still looking at the grid. The next day, Samir came to the staffroom door with another problem from the back of the book. "Sir, I want to try this one."

qa.q: What did Samir draw on the back of the paper?
qa.a: A grid.

qa.q: Why did Samir pack slowly, still looking at the grid?
qa.a: Samir seemed proud and thoughtful, taking in that the grid was good work, not luck, and that switching methods had paid off.

qa.q: Which choice by Francis sir mattered most under the time pressure?
qa.a: Stopping for a moment despite the crowded room and the notebooks, and naming Samir's exact strategy rather than just saying "well done".

qa.q: What would change if Francis sir had walked past without stopping?
qa.a: Samir might have left without knowing the grid idea was valuable, and might not have come to the staffroom asking for a harder problem.

grounding: Despite a crowded class and little time, a teacher praises a child's switch of strategy, and the child seeks more challenge.

passage: The school art exhibition was a week away, and every Class 9 student had to submit one drawing. Lokesh had no colours at home and only the lunch break to work in the crowded art room. He sketched a banyan tree, looked at Baljeet's page beside him, where a whole market scene was coming alive, and crumpled his paper. "I'm just not the creative type," he said. "Some people have it. I don't." Baljeet offered a spare pencil and said the tree trunk looked good. Lokesh shook his head. "Doesn't matter. I'll never be good at this." For the rest of the week he spent lunch in the canteen. On exhibition day his slot on the wall was empty, and he acted as if he didn't care.

qa.q: What did Lokesh sketch before crumpling the paper?
qa.a: A banyan tree.

qa.q: Why did Lokesh crumple his drawing after looking at Baljeet's page?
qa.a: Comparing his tree with Baljeet's market scene made him feel drawing is a gift he was born without, so trying seemed pointless and a bit humiliating.

qa.q: What could Lokesh have tried instead of giving up?
qa.a: Finishing the tree using Baljeet's spare pencil and the praise for the trunk, treating it as a starting level rather than a verdict.

qa.q: How might Baljeet feel seeing the empty slot on the wall?
qa.a: Baljeet may feel sad and a little helpless, having offered a pencil and real praise that Lokesh wouldn't accept.

grounding: A teenager who struggles with drawing decides he lacks creativity and stops, leaving his exhibition slot empty.

passage: Asif stood at the back of the Sunday sketching class in Mylapore, looking at his page. The temple gopuram he'd drawn leaned as if about to fall. "I'm just not creative," he told Karthik. "My hands don't do it." Karthik showed him his own sketchbook from last year: wobbly lines, a lopsided cow. "This was me in June." Asif glanced at it and shrugged. "You're different. You have it. I don't." The instructor suggested he try the gopuram again, one tier at a time. Asif closed his book. "No point." The next Sunday he didn't come. Karthik sent him a photo of the gopuram, drawn tier by tier. Asif left it unread.

qa.q: What did Karthik show Asif from last year?
qa.a: His own sketchbook: wobbly lines, a lopsided cow.

qa.q: Why did Asif shrug off Karthik's old sketchbook?
qa.a: Asif felt discouraged; believing drawing ability is something you either have or don't, he read Karthik's improvement as proof that Karthik was just different.

qa.q: What turning point did Asif miss, and what might have helped?
qa.a: The instructor's suggestion to redraw one tier at a time; trying it would have shown him his own drawing could improve.

qa.q: How might Karthik feel when the photo stays unread?
qa.a: Karthik may feel disappointed and shut out, having shared his own clumsy start to encourage a friend who won't listen.

grounding: A teenager decides he is simply not creative and quits sketching, turning his current level into a permanent limit.

passage:
"Shalini, where's your art project? It's due Monday."
"I'm not doing it, Amma."
Kavitha put down the vegetable knife. "Not doing it?"
"I can't draw. Everyone knows. Nithya draws like a real artist, and mine look like a baby's."
"You drew that beautiful kolam at Pongal."
"That's different. That's patterns. I'm not creative." Shalini pushed the sketchbook under the sofa. "Some people are born with it."
"Were you born reading?"
"What?"
"You couldn't read at three. Now you read my office letters for me."
Shalini frowned. "That's not the same."
"Maybe. Or maybe you're at the start of drawing, like you were once at the start of reading."
Shalini didn't answer, but she didn't push the sketchbook any further under, either.

qa.q: When is Shalini's art project due?
qa.a: On Monday.

qa.q: Why does Shalini say "Some people are born with it"?
qa.a: Shalini feels embarrassed next to Nithya, whose drawings look like a real artist's, and believing talent is inborn spares her from trying and failing.

qa.q: Which question from Kavitha might shift Shalini's view, and why?
qa.a: "Were you born reading?", because it reminds her of a skill she clearly built over time, suggesting drawing could grow too.

qa.q: How does Kavitha see her daughter's refusal?
qa.a: Kavitha doesn't accept "I'm not creative"; she sees a beginner, points to the kolam and to reading, and hopes Shalini will try.

grounding: A teenager decides she is not creative and stops, and her mother challenges the idea that talent is fixed.

passage:
"Tarun got the internship at the research lab," Mummy said at dinner, beaming. "Your cousin is doing so well!"
Nilesh put down the roti. "Great."
"You should call and congratulate him."
"Why? So he can tell me how easy it was?"
Papa looked up. "Nilesh."
"It is easy for him. He was born like that. Top of every class since he was six. Some people get the brain and some don't."
"You also applied to that lab," Mummy said gently.
"And didn't get in, because I'm not Tarun." Nilesh pushed the plate back. "Every time he wins something, it's a reminder of what I'll never be."
"Or," Papa said, "it's someone you could ask about how he prepared."
Nilesh stared at the plate. "Can I be excused?"

qa.q: What did Tarun get?
qa.a: The internship at the research lab.

qa.q: Why does Tarun's success feel like a loss to Nilesh?
qa.a: Nilesh feels jealous and inadequate: seeing talent as fixed at birth, he takes Tarun's win as proof of a gap that can never close.

qa.q: What choice does Papa suggest, and why might it help?
qa.a: Asking Tarun how he prepared, which would turn Tarun's success into information Nilesh could use instead of a threat.

qa.q: How might Mummy feel when Nilesh asks to be excused?
qa.a: Mummy likely feels sorry that her happy news hurt, and worried that Nilesh sees the cousin as a rival instead of a help.

grounding: A student sees a cousin's success as proof of fixed destiny and feels threatened rather than inspired.

passage: Suraj joined our hostel wing in second year, and within a month he'd won the college coding contest. I remember reading the notice on the board and feeling my stomach drop, as if something had been taken from me. I'd been coding since school. I told myself he was just a natural, that people like him are built differently, that I'd hit my ceiling. After that I avoided him. I stopped going to the coding club because he was always there. When he posted his solutions, I didn't read them. Looking back, I see it: every time he did well, I felt smaller, as if there were only so much talent in the world and he'd taken my share. A friend finally said, "Naveen, you could just ask him how he practises." I haven't yet. But I've gone back to the club.

qa.q: What did Suraj win within a month of joining the wing?
qa.a: The college coding contest.

qa.q: Why did Naveen's stomach drop on reading the notice?
qa.a: Naveen felt threatened and small, believing talent was fixed and limited, so Suraj's win seemed to take away Naveen's own share.

qa.q: What turning point helped Naveen, and what could be the next step?
qa.a: A friend's suggestion to ask Suraj how he practises; Naveen has returned to the club, and actually asking would turn envy into learning.

qa.q: How might Suraj have experienced Naveen avoiding him?
qa.a: Suraj may have noticed a fellow coder pulling away without knowing why, and might have welcomed a chance to share his practice.

grounding: A student sees a peer's win as proof of a fixed gap and feels threatened, then begins to shift.

passage:
Faculty advisor's note, Nirmala, Music department, 9 February
Tenzin came to see me after the semester recital. His classmate Dorjee played the solo and got a standing ovation; Tenzin was in the second row of the ensemble. He told me, "Dorjee was born with it. I'll never play like that, so what's the point of practising?" He said he can't bear to hear Dorjee rehearse anymore and has started booking practice rooms at the far end of the building. He looked less angry than defeated. I remember Dorjee's first-year recordings; they were ordinary.
What I did next: I played Tenzin one of those recordings and asked him to set one small practice goal for the month. I also suggested he ask Dorjee how he practises. We meet again in two weeks.

qa.q: Where did Dorjee play at the recital?
qa.a: Dorjee played the solo and got a standing ovation.

qa.q: Why can't Tenzin bear to hear Dorjee rehearse?
qa.a: Seeing the gap as inborn makes every note from Dorjee feel like proof of Tenzin's own limit, so it stings rather than inspires.

qa.q: Which choice by Nirmala might change Tenzin's view, and why?
qa.a: Playing Dorjee's ordinary first-year recording, since it shows the skill was built over time and gives Tenzin a reason to set his own practice goal.

qa.q: How might Dorjee react if Tenzin asked how he practises?
qa.a: Dorjee might be pleased to be asked and happy to share, and could become a help rather than a threat.

grounding: An advisor notes a student who sees a peer's talent as destiny and feels defeated, and shows him the peer's early work.
